title: How to Check Email Only Twice a Day Without Missing Urgent Mail
meta_description: Learn how to check email only twice a day without missing urgent mail: two fixed windows, VIP alerts in Gmail and Outlook, and a 2-week trial.
quick_answer: To check email only twice a day, book two fixed windows, such as 11:00 and 16:00, and close email in between. Turn off all email notifications, then re-enable alerts for a handful of key senders in Gmail or Outlook and test them. Ask your team to phone or message you about anything urgent. In each window, delete, delegate, do or defer every message, and trial it for two weeks.
key_takeaways: Book two fixed email windows, such as 11:00 and 16:00, as repeating calendar events. Quit email completely between them.
Turn off every email notification, then turn alerts back on for three to five key senders only. Send a test email to check they work.
Agree with your manager and team that anything urgent comes by phone or chat, not email.
In each window, make one decision on every message: delete, delegate, do or defer.
Run a two-week trial and keep a simple log. If two windows feels risky, start with three and cut back later.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for knowledge workers, such as analysts, writers, developers, consultants and managers, who don't have to reply instantly and want longer stretches of focused work without missing anything that really can't wait.
intro:
Checking email all day feels responsive. For most knowledge workers, though, it breaks the day into pieces too small for serious work. Checking email only twice a day fixes that, as long as you build a backup so truly urgent issues still reach you.

This guide covers the full setup: choosing your two windows, turning off notifications, allowing alerts from key senders in Gmail and Outlook, agreeing an urgency rule with your team and clearing your inbox quickly. It ends with a two-week trial plan so you can judge the change on evidence. It's also honest about who shouldn't try it.

steps.name: Choose two fixed email windows
steps.text: Pick two times that repeat every working day, such as 11:00–11:45 and 16:00–16:45. Book them as repeating calendar events called 'Email window'. Choose times that match when your colleagues and clients usually send email and expect answers.

steps.name: Turn off every email notification
steps.text: Turn off new-mail banners, sounds and badges in your desktop email app, your browser and your phone's mail app. Then nothing can pull you into your inbox between windows. Leave calendar reminders on so you don't miss meetings.

steps.name: Turn alerts back on for key senders only, then test them
steps.text: Choose three to five people who really can't wait. In Gmail, create a filter that always marks their messages as important, then set notifications to important or high priority only. In Outlook, create a rule that shows a desktop alert for those senders, or limit mobile notifications to Favourite People. Ask one of them to send you a test email.

steps.name: Agree an 'urgent means call or message' rule
steps.text: Tell your manager and team that anything that can't wait until your next window should come by phone or chat, and name the exact channel. Present it as a two-week experiment to protect focus time.

steps.name: Add a response-time line to your signature (optional)
steps.text: For people outside your team, add a line such as 'I check email around 11:00 and 16:00. For anything urgent, call [number].' Skip it if it might make you look slow to clients.

steps.name: Close email between windows
steps.text: Quit the desktop app rather than minimising it. Close webmail tabs and move your phone's mail app off the home screen, so checking takes a deliberate effort.

steps.name: Clear the inbox with delete, delegate, do, defer
steps.text: In each window, open each message once. Delete or archive it, delegate it, do it now if it takes about two minutes, or defer it to your task list or calendar. Stop when the window ends.

steps.name: Run a two-week trial and review
steps.text: For 14 days, log how often you check email outside your windows, how long each window takes, any near misses and how many focus blocks you complete. On day 14, choose whether to keep two windows, move to three, or change your key-sender list.

sections.heading: Is checking email twice a day right for your role?
paragraphs: Checking email only twice a day suits you if most of your email can wait a few hours without harming anyone or holding up their work. That describes many analysts, writers, developers, designers, researchers, consultants and managers. Their real output comes from focused project work, not quick replies.

The benefit is fewer interruptions. Every look at your inbox pulls your attention away from the task in front of you, and a 'quick check' often turns into a thread you never planned to deal with. Two scheduled windows replace dozens of small interruptions with two planned sessions.

This approach doesn't suit customer support, sales roles that handle incoming leads, on-call or incident roles, executive assistants, or anyone who has promised a set response time. If you're judged on how fast you reply, you can still use the tactics here (key-sender alerts, batching and the four Ds) with shorter, more frequent windows. Either way, talk to your manager before you change anything.
bullets: Would a four- or five-hour wait on a typical email cause real harm, such as a missed deadline, a lost deal or a colleague who can't move forward?
Can people already reach you faster in a real emergency, by phone, Teams or Slack?
Are you judged mainly on your output rather than on how fast you reply?
Are you the only person who can act on something time-critical? If so, arrange cover or a backup first.

sections.heading: How to check email only twice a day: choose your two windows
paragraphs: To check email only twice a day, pick two fixed times each working day, usually one late in the morning and one mid-afternoon, and protect them like meetings. A common pattern is 11:00–11:45 and 16:00–16:45. The right times depend on when your colleagues and clients send email and expect answers.

A late-morning window keeps your first hours free for focused work and still catches overnight and early messages before lunch. A mid-afternoon window leaves time to reply before others finish for the day, so requests don't wait overnight for no reason.

Start with 45 minutes per window and adjust after a week of tracking. Book both as repeating calendar events called 'Email window'. Colleagues can then see your routine, and you won't accept meetings over them by mistake.
Keep calendar reminders switched on. They're separate from new-mail alerts, so closing your inbox doesn't mean missing a meeting.
bullets: Typical 9-to-5: 11:00 and 16:00.
Early starter: 10:00 and 15:00.
Team across time zones: one window near the start of your shared hours and one near the end.
Mondays and your first day back from leave: make the first window longer to clear the backlog.

sections.heading: Turn off notifications, then allow alerts from key senders in Gmail and Outlook
paragraphs: Turn off every email notification first. Then turn alerts back on only for the handful of people who really can't wait, usually your manager, one or two key clients and anyone covering for you. Google and Microsoft often rename and move their menus, so use the paths below as a guide and check them in each app's help pages.

Gmail: In Gmail on the web, open Settings, choose See all settings, and on the General tab set desktop notifications to either off or 'Important mail notifications on'. In the Gmail mobile app, open your account's notification settings and choose None or High priority only. Both 'important' options rely on Gmail's importance markers. To make your key senders count, create a filter with their email addresses, tick 'Always mark it as important' and 'Never send it to Spam', and apply a label such as VIP. Gmail also marks some other messages as important on its own, so expect the odd extra alert. On Android, you may be able to turn on notifications for a single label, which gives you tighter control.

Outlook: In classic Outlook for Windows, go to File > Options > Mail. Under message arrival, untick the sound, the envelope icon and Display a Desktop Alert. Then create a rule for messages from your key senders with the action 'display a Desktop Alert'. In the new Outlook and Outlook on the web, notification controls are under Settings, so check whether your version can limit alerts to favourite people. The Outlook mobile app usually lets you limit email notifications to Favourite People, so add your key senders as favourites first.

Your phone is your backup. Focus modes on iPhone and Do Not Disturb on Android both let calls and messages from chosen people through while silencing everything else. That fits well with an 'urgent means call' rule. Windows and macOS have similar focus settings for your computer.

If the built-in settings aren't precise enough, an automation tool such as Zapier or Make can forward emails from specific senders to Slack, Teams or another chat app. Check with your IT team first, because many employers limit connecting work email to outside services.
bullets: Keep your key-sender list to three to five names. If it keeps growing, you're bringing back constant interruptions.
Only include automated alerts, such as outage notices, if you're the person who has to respond.
Ask someone on your list to send a test email, and check that the alert arrives on both your computer and your phone.
Review the list on day 14 of your trial.

sections.heading: Agree an 'urgent means call or message' rule (with templates)
paragraphs: Your most important backup is a rule your team shares: if something can't wait until your next email window, people call or send a chat message instead of emailing. Email then becomes the channel for everything that can wait a few hours, which is most of it.

Raise it with your manager first, as a two-week experiment to protect focus time, then share it with your team. Define urgent clearly: something that will hold someone up or cause a problem before your next window. Name the exact channel, such as a phone call or a direct message in Teams or Slack. Offer the same in return so colleagues know how to reach you quickly.

A signature line is optional, but it helps people outside your team who don't know your routine. Skip it if it might make you look slow to clients, and check whether your organisation has rules about signatures. Avoid an automatic reply that's always on, because it adds clutter to every thread.
bullets: Manager pitch: “I'd like to try two fixed email windows for two weeks to protect focus time. Your emails will still alert me straight away, and I'll share what I learn at the end.”
Team message: “For the next two weeks I'm checking email at 11:00 and 16:00. If something needs me sooner, please call me or message me on [Teams/Slack]. For everything else, email as usual.”
Signature line: “I check email around 11:00 and 16:00 [time zone]. For anything urgent, call [number] or message me on [channel].”
Shorter version: “I reply to email within one working day. Urgent? Call [number].”

sections.heading: Clear the inbox in each window: delete, delegate, do, defer
paragraphs: In each email window, open every new message once and make one of four decisions: delete (or archive), delegate, do or defer. The goal is for every message to have a decision before the window closes, even if the work it creates happens later.
Start with anything from your key senders, then work through the rest. In long threads, read the newest message first so you don't reply to something that's already been settled.

A few changes to your setup make every window faster. Create 'Action' and 'Waiting for' labels or folders, learn the keyboard shortcuts for archiving and replying, and save templates for replies you send often. Gmail and Outlook both let you save reusable text, though the feature names depend on your version.
When the window ends, stop. If you often can't finish, make the window longer, unsubscribe from more emails, or ask whether you really need to be on so many threads.
bullets: Delete or archive anything that needs no action, such as FYI threads, newsletters and copies you don't need. Unsubscribe from repeat senders as you go.
Delegate when someone else is better placed to deal with it. Forward it with a clear request and deadline, then file the original under 'Waiting for'.
Do it now if it takes about two minutes or less. This is the 'two-minute rule' from David Allen's book Getting Things Done.
Defer anything that needs real work. Add it to your task list or calendar, then archive it or file it under 'Action'. Don't use your inbox as a to-do list.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls and how to fix them
paragraphs: Most problems in the first few weeks come from habits and edge cases, not from the method itself, and each one has a simple fix.
bullets: People still email you urgent requests: reply briefly and point them to the urgent channel, then remind the team at your next meeting.
You keep checking anyway: move mail off your phone's home screen, sign out of webmail and quit the desktop app rather than minimising it.
You need a login code or password-reset email: search for it, use it and close email without scanning your inbox.
Windows keep running over: unsubscribe from emails you don't need, leave threads you don't need to be on and save templates for common replies.
Your manager is uneasy: share your trial log and offer a temporary third window or a short lunchtime check for key senders.

sections.heading: Run a two-week trial and measure what changes
paragraphs: Treat the change as a 14-day experiment with simple measurements. That way, you decide based on evidence rather than on the anxiety of not checking.

Day 0 (about an hour): Book your windows, turn off notifications, set up and test key-sender alerts, send your team message and add the signature line if you're using one. On one normal day before you start, count how often you check email. That count is your starting point.

Days 1–7: Stick to your windows and keep a simple log on paper, in a spreadsheet or in a Notion page. The urge to check is usually strongest in the first few days. At the end of week one, change your window times or length once.
Days 8–14: Keep your settings the same so the results are reliable. Ask your manager and one or two close colleagues whether they noticed any problems.

On day 14, use a simple rule. If there were no serious near misses and you completed more focus blocks, keep going. If something urgent was missed, check whether it came through the agreed channel. If it didn't, the fix is usually clearer communication, not more checking.
bullets: How many times you checked email outside your windows, compared with your starting count.
How many minutes each window took, and whether you finished.
Near misses: anything that needed you sooner, and how it reached you in the end.
How many uninterrupted focus blocks of 60 minutes or more you completed each day.
A 1–5 score for your focus at the end of each day, plus any feedback from colleagues.

sections.heading: If two windows feels risky, start with three
paragraphs: If two windows feels like too big a jump, start with three (morning, midday and late afternoon) and drop to two once you've seen that nothing goes wrong. For example, try 9:30, 13:00 and 16:30 for 20–30 minutes each, so your total email time stays about the same.

Three windows is not a failure. In a 2015 experiment, University of British Columbia researchers Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth Dunn found that people who limited email checking to three times a day reported lower daily stress than when they checked whenever they liked. Checking in planned batches matters more than the exact number of windows.

Another middle option is two full windows plus a five-minute lunchtime check of your VIP label or favourites view only. Deal with anything critical, then close the app without looking at the rest of your inbox.
bullets: Three windows: 9:30, 13:00 and 16:30, for 20–30 minutes each.
Two windows plus a key-sender check: full windows at 11:00 and 16:00, plus a five-minute VIP-only check at 13:00.
Busy weeks, such as launches or deadlines: add a window for that week, then go back to two.

recommendations.best_for: Keeping your two-week trial log, a simple task list for deferred emails and a weekly plan of email windows and focus blocks, all in one workspace.
recommendations.not_for: People already happy with their calendar and task app, or anyone looking for a tool that controls email notifications, which Notion doesn't do. Check current plans and AI features on Notion's website.

recommendations.best_for: Forwarding emails from a short list of key senders to Slack, Teams or another chat app when the alerts built into Gmail or Outlook aren't precise enough. You can set it up without writing code.
recommendations.not_for: People whose built-in alerts already work, or whose employer doesn't allow work email to be connected to outside tools. Check with IT first, and confirm current plans and pricing on Zapier's website.

recommendations.best_for: People who prefer a visual, flowchart-style builder, or who already use Make, and want the same key-sender forwarding with extra filtering steps.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who only needs one simple alert, which is easier with built-in settings, or who doesn't have IT approval to connect work email. Confirm current plans and supported apps on Make's website.

faq.question: Is it realistic to check email only twice a day?
faq.answer: For many knowledge workers, yes, as long as the role doesn't require instant replies and colleagues have a faster way to reach them in an emergency. It works best with alerts for the few senders who can't wait and a team agreement that urgent means call or message. Customer support, sales and on-call roles usually need to check more often.

faq.question: What are the best times to check email twice a day?
faq.answer: Many people use one window late in the morning and one mid-afternoon, such as 11:00 and 16:00. That keeps early focus time free and still lets you reply before colleagues finish for the day. Adjust the times for your team's time zones and for when your key contacts usually email.

faq.question: How do I make sure I don't miss urgent emails?
faq.answer: Set up alerts for a short list of key senders and test them. In Gmail, use a filter that marks their emails as important, plus important or high-priority notifications. In Outlook, use a desktop-alert rule or Favourite People notifications. More importantly, agree with your team that anything truly urgent comes by phone or chat, and log any near misses during your trial.

faq.question: Should I check email first thing in the morning?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Starting with email tends to fill your morning with other people's priorities, so many people do an hour or two of focused work before their first window. If key colleagues or clients are in time zones ahead of yours, a short early window may make more sense, so test it during your trial.

faq.question: What if my boss expects fast replies?
faq.answer: Talk to your manager before you start. Present it as a two-week experiment to protect focus time, and confirm that their emails will still alert you straight away. Share your log at the end. If fast email replies are a core part of your job, use three or more windows instead.

faq.question: Does checking email less often reduce stress?
faq.answer: There is some evidence that it can. In a 2015 study, University of British Columbia researchers Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth Dunn found that people asked to check email only three times a day reported lower daily stress than in a week when they checked as often as they liked. Results vary by person and role, so your own two-week log is the best guide.

conclusion: Checking email only twice a day isn't about ignoring people. It gives email a fixed place in your day and a reliable route for the few things that can't wait. Choose two windows, turn off notifications, allow alerts from a handful of key senders, agree that urgent means call or message, and make one decision on each email. Then run the two-week trial, read your log and keep what works, whether that's two windows, three, or two plus a quick lunchtime check for key senders.
